title: Serving runtime: kernel scheduling, profiling playbook, and benchmarking suite
author: Rohit Patel
body:
Summary:
This document consolidates the serving runtime design notes for kernel scheduling, an operational profiling playbook, the standard benchmarking suite we run in CI and nightly performance jobs, recent release highlights affecting the runtime, a curated list of known issues and mitigations, and the runbooks used by the on-call/runtime team. It is intended as the canonical reference for engineers troubleshooting performance regressions, onboarding to the runtime, and maintaining the benchmarking harness.

Goals / audience:
- Audience: runtime engineers, infra SREs, performance engineers, model-onboarding engineers.
- Goals: make it straightforward to reproduce, profile, triage, and fix performance and memory regressions; provide operational runbooks for incidents; document our benchmarking methodology for tracking upstream changes.

1) Runtime architecture summary
- Components:
  - Frontend (request router): validates request, enforces quotas, applies routing policy.
  - Batch coalescer + scheduler: groups compatible requests, builds execution batches, decides kernel sequence and device placement.
  - Inference engine (serving runtime): executes kernels, manages KV cache, performs quantized ops when configured.
  - Telemetry/logging: token-level latency traces, nvtx markers, per-model token counters, and resource metrics via DCGM.
- Key design constraints: predictable p99 latency, high GPU utilization for throughput workloads, graceful degradation (fallback to smaller model or CPU pool), and memory isolation between workspaces/customers.
- SLOs (examples, enforced at product/infra boundary):
  - Small-chat model (gpt-small-8k v1): p95 <= 120 ms per request, p99 <= 300 ms, throughput >= 350 tokens/s per GPU@batching config.
  - Large decoding model (gpt-large-32k v2, single token streaming): p95 <= 250 ms, p99 <= 1.2s.
  - Memory safety: < 85% GPU memory utilization on baseline traffic for autoscale headroom.

2) Kernel scheduling design (high level)
- Goals: minimize p99 while keeping high aggregate throughput; adapt to variable sequence lengths; prevent head-of-line blocking; prioritize interactive traffic.
- Inputs to scheduler: request priority (interactive vs batch), model variant (quantized vs fp16), max sequence length, KV cache hit rate, target latency SLO, current GPU occupancy, and model-specific kernel profiles.
- Scheduling primitives:
  - Priority lanes: requests are assigned lanes (interactive-high, interactive-low, batch) with configurable concurrency limits.
  - Sequence-length bucketing: requests are grouped by effective decode length to avoid padding blow-up. Typical buckets: short (<=128), medium (129-1024), long (>1024).
  - Kernel fusion and re-ordering: where applicable, the scheduler prefers fused kernels for repeated patterns (attention + ffw), falling back when fusion isn't available for the layer shape.
  - Batch size caps: model-configured max_batch (default 64), and a dynamic per-GPU cap based on observed latency tail.
  - KV cache locality: allocate and pin KV cache ranges per stream when reuse probability exceeds 30% to avoid eviction churn.
- Example policy (interactive traffic):
  1. Assign to interactive-high lane if request SLO <= 200ms and model is available in fp16/quantized variants.
  2. If batchable (same model and compatible tokenizer/stop sequences), coalesce up to interactive_batch_target (default 8) or until interactive_latency_budget (default 20 ms) expires.
  3. Dispatch with kernel sequence chosen by model kernel-profile table (see kernel-profiles repo).

3) Profiling playbook (step-by-step)
- When to profile: unexpected p95/p99 increases, memory OOMs, regression after kernel or CUDA dependency changes, or model onboarding with new architecture.
- Tools we use: NVIDIA Nsight Systems (nsys), NVIDIA Nsight Compute (ncu), gpustat / dcgm-exporter, nvidia-smi, Linux perf, py-spy / pprof for CPU stacks, and the runtime's built-in trace (nvtx markers + JSON trace export).

- Quick checklist before collecting data:
  1. Reproduce the issue in a staging environment that mirrors production hardware (same GPU type, driver version, and CUDA/cuDNN versions).
  2. Ensure the test uses identical model weights, tokenizer, and input distribution (use benchmark dataset described below).
  3. Confirm system counters have a baseline: run 60s of steady-state traffic and capture gpustat/dcgm for baseline.

- Collect traces (recommended sequence):
  1. Lightweight telemetry: run gpustat -cp 5 and collect `nvidia-smi --query-gpu=utilization.gpu,utilization.memory,memory.total,memory.used --format=csv -l 1 -f /tmp/gpu_metrics.csv` for 60–180s.
  2. NVTX + runtime JSON: enable runtime tracing (RUNTIME_TRACE=nvtx,json) and run the workload to produce the per-request JSON trace.
  3. Nsight Systems (wall-clock / concurrency):
     - Command: `nsys profile -o /tmp/nsys_trace --trace=cuda,nvtx,osrt -t 60 --capture-range=nvtx python -m bench.runner --config examples/interactive_small.yaml`
     - Notes: use --capture-range=nvtx to limit trace size for production-like loads.
  4. Nsight Compute (kernel-level): select the slow kernel(s) from the nsys summary and run ncu for one or a few invocations: `ncu --target-processes all -o /tmp/ncu_report <binary> --model ...`.
  5. Per-GPU perf counters: use DCGM or `nvidia-smi dmon` for aggregated counters if available on hardware.
  6. CPU sampling (if host-side queuing is suspected): `py-spy record -o /tmp/pyspy.svg -- python -m bench.runner --config ...` and/or `perf record -F 99 -g -- <cmd>` followed by `perf report`.

- Analyze traces:
  - Use the nsys timeline to identify periods of GPU idle while host-side queuing has requests pending (sign of host bottleneck).
  - Identify kernels with high average latency or low SM occupancy in ncu; check for memory-bound vs compute-bound patterns.
  - Inspect NVTX markers emitted by the runtime to map high-level operations (batching, KV load, decode loop) to kernels.
  - Correlate p95/p99 spikes to kernel launches and memory usage; check for out-of-memory activity or allocator retries.

- Example actionable findings and fixes:
  - Observation: long gaps between kernels with GPU utilization low and host threads using 100% CPU -> Fix: increase host worker threads or reduce expensive Python work in request pipeline (move tokenization to C++/Rust bundle).
  - Observation: kernel fusion unavailable for certain layer shapes -> Fix: add specialized fused kernel or fallback kernel optimization; update kernel-profile thresholds.
  - Observation: frequent KV eviction -> Fix: increase per-GPU KV reservation (default 4GB -> 6GB) or change caching policy to LRU per-workspace.

4) Benchmarking suite (how we measure and track regressions)
- Purpose: reproduce representative workloads, track p50/p95/p99 latency and throughput across model variants and hardware, and surface regressions via PR gating and nightly benchmarks.
- Test categories:
  - Microbench: isolated kernels and small end-to-end model runs (single GPU, synthetic input).
  - Interactive latency: sampled user-like requests (short/medium/long sequence distributions).
  - Throughput: sustained decode workload (multi-stream, max batching) to measure tokens/sec and GPU efficiency.
  - Memory stress: large-batch and long-context tests to validate KV cache behaviour and OOM thresholds.
- Canonical workloads (examples):
  - chat-short: 90% short (<=64 tokens), 10% medium, batch target=8, replication=1.
  - multi-turn: include KV cache hits with warm cache probabilities at 60/80/95%.
  - long-context: 8K and 32K sequence profiles for models supporting long context.
- Metrics collected: p50/p95/p99 latency, tail latency distribution, tokens/sec, GPU utilization, memory used, page-faults, kernel-level durations.
- Benchmark CI integration:
  - PRs touching runtime/KERNEL files must run the microbench suite (`ci/bench/microbench.sh`) with baselines stored in S3 (`s3://redwood-bench/baseline/$(git rev-parse --short HEAD)`).
  - Nightly job: runs full suite across 3 hardware tiers (A100-80GB, H100-80GB, RTX6000) and uploads results to the perf dashboard (Grafana panel: runtime/benchmarks).
- Example benchmark config (YAML snippet as text):
  - name: chat-short
    model: gpt-small-8k-v1
    input_distribution: samples/chat-short.json
    concurrency: 16
    batch_target: 8
    duration_s: 300

5) Recent runtime release notes (high level)
- v2026.01.12: kernel scheduling improvements
  - Introduced adaptive interactive preemption (preempt large-batch kernels when interactive-high requests arrive).
  - Reduced p99 for chat-short by ~18% on A100 in nightly benchmarks.
  - Added NVTX markers for KV-load and cache-evict events in the runtime trace.
- v2026.02.02: kernel selection update
  - Improved kernel-profile table resolution for attention shapes; fallback path has reduced memory copies.
  - Fixed a host-side queuing bug that could cause worker-thread starvation under bursty traffic.

6) Known issues and mitigations
- Issue: occasional p99 spikes when model is served in mixed-precision (FP16) under heavy long-context traffic.
  - Symptoms: p99 spikes, GPU memory climbs then OOMs after several minutes.
  - Mitigation: pin to FP32 or quantized variant for long-context customers; increase reserved KV memory; limit concurrent long-context streams per GPU.
- Issue: Nsight traces overflow disk rapidly on high-QPS workloads.
  - Mitigation: use capture-range=nvtx and shorter capture windows; rely on aggregated telemetry for long-term debugging.
- Issue: nvtx markers missing for some third-party fused kernels.
  - Mitigation: update kernel wrapper to emit NVTX at kernel entry/exit; ensure build-time macro ENABLE_NVTX is set.
- Issue: faintly higher p95 after CUDA 12.x driver update on H100.
  - Mitigation: lock driver to validated version for production (12.1.x), run smoke on canary fleet, and roll drivers with canary ratio 5% -> 25% -> 100%.

7) Runbooks (operational playbooks)
- High p99 latency (interactive):
  1. Confirm alert: check Grafana (runtime/latency) and Incidents slack channel.
  2. Check recent deploys: `git log -n 5 --pretty=oneline` on runtime repo and consult Deployment Service.
  3. Collect lightweight metrics: `gpustat -cp 5`, `curl http://metrics/runtime/last-5m?model=...` and runtime trace for 60s.
  4. If host-side CPU is 100%: scale up workers on host (systemd restart runtime-workers@{N+2}) or reduce batch_target.
  5. If GPU kernels are slow: run nsys capture for 60s, analyze hot kernels and open a ticket (runtime-kernel) with ncu summary.
  6. Escalation: if p99 impact > 10% of production traffic for > 5 minutes, page runtime on-call (oncall-runtime) and SRE lead.
- GPU OOMs / memory pressure:
  1. Identify OOM logs in Sentry / logstash: search for "CUDA out of memory" and gather trace id.
  2. Evacuate affected model instances: disable route for model variant, fallback to smaller model or quantized variant.
  3. Increase per-GPU KV reservation or reduce max_batch for the model.
  4. If recurring: schedule model memory profile, collect nsys and memory allocations, and add JIRA ticket for model quantization or kernel memory fix.

8) Team wiki / repos / ownership
- Runtime repositories: `github.com/redwoodinc/serving-runtime` (core), `github.com/redwoodinc/kernel-profiles` (kernel selection table), `github.com/redwoodinc/bench` (benchmark harness).
- Dashboards: Grafana (runtime/overview, runtime/benchmarks, runtime/latency-by-model).
- On-call: runtime on-call rotation is documented in `eng-oncall/calendar` and uses PagerDuty schedule "runtime-oncall".
- Pager / escalation: runtime on-call -> SRE lead -> infra eng manager.
- Owners: runtime team (primary), eng-sre (secondary). For kernel work, assign to kernel-performance subteam (owner: Marcus Lee).

9) References and related pages
- See also: serving-runtime-comprehensive-2026 (architecture deep dive), serving-runtime-runbooks-and-playbook-2026 (runbook index), benchmarking-and-perf-suite-2026 (bench harness details).
- Kernel profiles are stored in the kernel-profiles repo and a canonical table is exported to S3: s3://redwood-kernels/profiles/latest.csv.

Appendix: quick commands
- Lightweight metrics: `gpustat -cp` and `nvidia-smi --query-gpu=memory.used,utilization.gpu --format=csv -l 1`
- Capture NSYS: `nsys profile -o /tmp/nsys_trace --trace=cuda,nvtx -t 60 --capture-range=nvtx python -m bench.runner --config examples/interactive_small.yaml`
- Capture NCU for a specific kernel: `ncu --target-processes all -o /tmp/ncu_report --kernel-id <id> <cmd>`
- Run microbench in CI: `ci/bench/microbench.sh --model gpt-small-8k-v1`

If you find a gap in this playbook (missing tools, unclear thresholds, or untracked workloads), open a PR against this page and assign reviewers `Elena Martinez` and `Marcus Lee`.
